# Introduction

Hierarchical data is surprisingly common, and are commonly represented in `<svg aria-hidden="true" role="img" viewBox="0 0 581 512" style="height:1em;width:1.13em;vertical-align:-0.125em;margin-left:auto;margin-right:auto;font-size:inherit;fill:currentColor;overflow:visible;position:relative;"><path d="M581 226.6C581 119.1 450.9 32 290.5 32S0 119.1 0 226.6C0 322.4 103.3 402 239.4 418.1V480h99.1v-61.5c24.3-2.7 47.6-7.4 69.4-13.9L448 480h112l-67.4-113.7c54.5-35.4 88.4-84.9 88.4-139.7zm-466.8 14.5c0-73.5 98.9-133 220.8-133s211.9 40.7 211.9 133c0 50.1-26.5 85-70.3 106.4-2.4-1.6-4.7-2.9-6.4-3.7-10.2-5.2-27.8-10.5-27.8-10.5s86.6-6.4 86.6-92.7-90.6-87.9-90.6-87.9h-199V361c-74.1-21.5-125.2-67.1-125.2-119.9zm225.1 38.3v-55.6c57.8 0 87.8-6.8 87.8 27.3 0 36.5-38.2 28.3-87.8 28.3zm-.9 72.5H365c10.8 0 18.9 11.7 24 19.2-16.1 1.9-33 2.8-50.6 2.9v-22.1z"/></svg>`{=html} by nested lists.

Broadcasted operations can be performed over dimensions, but not through nesting or hierarchies.  
Therefore, it is useful to be able to cast nested lists into dimensional lists.  
The 'broadcast' package provides the [cast_hier2dim()](/man/cast_hier2dim.qmd) function, to cast nested lists into dimensional lists, and the [cast_dim2hier()](/man/cast_dim2hier.qmd) to cast dimensional lists back to nested lists.

Casting between nested and dimensional lists is not only useful for broadcasting, however.  
Casting nested lists to dimensional lists has its own merits, as dimensional lists have some advantages over nested lists beside the broadcasting, such as the following:

 - Performing sub-set operations on **multiple** recursive subsets (using the `[[` and `[[<-` operators) requires a (potentially slow) loop, whereas multi-dimensional subsets (using operator forms like `[..., ...]` and `[..., ...]<-`) are vectorized and generally much faster.
 - Re-organizing recursive arrays is generally much easier, faster, and more straight-forward than re-organizing nested lists.
 
 
This Vignette explains the functions 'broadcast' provides to cast between nested and dimensional lists.

 


# Cast Nested List to Dimensional List

## Introduction

The [cast_hier2dim()](/man/cast_hier2dim.qmd) function casts a nested list into a dimensional list.  
This section gently introduces the properties of this function through a series of examples, where the complexity of each subsequent example increases a bit.  
Familiarity with nested lists and dimensional lists (i.e. arrays of type `list`) is essential to follow these examples.

 

## Example 1: Basics

For a first example, consider the following list:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
x <- list(
  group1 = list(
    class1 = list(
      height = rnorm(10, 170),
      weight = rnorm(10, 80),
      sex = sample(c("M", "F", NA), 10, TRUE)
    ),
    class2 = list(
      height = rnorm(10, 170),
      weight = rnorm(10, 80),
      sex = sample(c("M", "F", NA), 10, TRUE)
    )
  ),
  group2 = list(
    class1 = list(
      height = rnorm(10, 170),
      weight = rnorm(10, 80),
      sex = sample(c("M", "F", NA), 10, TRUE)
    ),
    class2 = list(
      height = rnorm(10, 170),
      weight = rnorm(10, 80),
      sex = sample(c("M", "F", NA), 10, TRUE)
    )
  )
)

```
:::



Before actually casting `x` into a dimensional list, one may want to know what the dimensions will become when casted as a dimensional list;  
The [hier2dim()](/man/cast_hier2dim.qmd) function shows you that:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
hier2dim(x)
#> no padding no padding no padding 
#>          3          2          2
```
:::


It returns the dimensions `c(3, 2, 2)`.  

Let's now cast `x` as a dimensional list:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
x2 <- cast_hier2dim(x) # actually cast nested list into dimensional list
print(x2)
#> , , 1
#> 
#>      [,1]         [,2]        
#> [1,] numeric,10   numeric,10  
#> [2,] numeric,10   numeric,10  
#> [3,] character,10 character,10
#> 
#> , , 2
#> 
#>      [,1]         [,2]        
#> [1,] numeric,10   numeric,10  
#> [2,] numeric,10   numeric,10  
#> [3,] character,10 character,10
```
:::


Using the default arguments, element `x[[i]][[j]][[k]]` corresponds to element `x2[k, j, i]` (for all `i`, `j`, and `k`).  
This can be changed, as will be shown in a later example.


As shown in the results above, [cast_hier2dim()](/man/cast_hier2dim.qmd) will obviously not preserve names.

In this case, it is trivially easy to set the `dimnames` of `x2`:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# remember: element `x[[i]][[j]][[k]]` corresponds to element `x2[k, j, i]`
# so we go from the deepest names to the surface names
dimnames(x2) <- list(
  names(x[[1]][[1]]),
  names(x[[1]]),
  names(x)
)
print(x2)
#> , , group1
#> 
#>        class1       class2      
#> height numeric,10   numeric,10  
#> weight numeric,10   numeric,10  
#> sex    character,10 character,10
#> 
#> , , group2
#> 
#>        class1       class2      
#> height numeric,10   numeric,10  
#> weight numeric,10   numeric,10  
#> sex    character,10 character,10
```
:::


There, the names are now correct.

As shown above, `<svg aria-hidden="true" role="img" viewBox="0 0 581 512" style="height:1em;width:1.13em;vertical-align:-0.125em;margin-left:auto;margin-right:auto;font-size:inherit;fill:currentColor;overflow:visible;position:relative;"><path d="M581 226.6C581 119.1 450.9 32 290.5 32S0 119.1 0 226.6C0 322.4 103.3 402 239.4 418.1V480h99.1v-61.5c24.3-2.7 47.6-7.4 69.4-13.9L448 480h112l-67.4-113.7c54.5-35.4 88.4-84.9 88.4-139.7zm-466.8 14.5c0-73.5 98.9-133 220.8-133s211.9 40.7 211.9 133c0 50.1-26.5 85-70.3 106.4-2.4-1.6-4.7-2.9-6.4-3.7-10.2-5.2-27.8-10.5-27.8-10.5s86.6-6.4 86.6-92.7-90.6-87.9-90.6-87.9h-199V361c-74.1-21.5-125.2-67.1-125.2-119.9zm225.1 38.3v-55.6c57.8 0 87.8-6.8 87.8 27.3 0 36.5-38.2 28.3-87.8 28.3zm-.9 72.5H365c10.8 0 18.9 11.7 24 19.2-16.1 1.9-33 2.8-50.6 2.9v-22.1z"/></svg>`{=html} will display a dimensional list more compactly than a nested list.  
Depending on the situation this may be either be desirable or undesirable.  

One can print `x2` less compactly without much effort by flattening it, using the [cast_dim2flat()](/man/cast_dim2flat.qmd) function.  
We only need to see a portion of the list in detail, so let's look at class1 from group 1 in the flattened form:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
cast_dim2flat(x2[, 1, "group1", drop = FALSE])
#> $`['height', 'class1', 'group1']`
#>  [1] 169.8534 170.3045 169.9818 170.3428 169.8843 168.6264 168.5645 170.5286
#>  [9] 170.1717 169.6173
#> 
#> $`['weight', 'class1', 'group1']`
#>  [1] 78.50220 78.72941 78.16260 78.62757 79.83542 80.39776 80.35968 81.39560
#>  [9] 79.30248 80.72435
#> 
#> $`['sex', 'class1', 'group1']`
#>  [1] "M" "M" NA  "F" NA  "M" "F" "F" "F" NA
```
:::



 

## Example 2: Cast from outside to inside


In Example 1, the default arguments were used for [cast_hier2dim()](/man/cast_hier2dim.qmd).  
One of these arguments is `in2out`, which defaults to `TRUE`.

Consider a nested list `x` with a depth of 3, and a dimensional list `X2` with 3 dimensions, where the relationship between `x` and `x2` can be expressed as `x2 <- cast_hier2dim(x, ...)`.  
Given this, the following can be stated about `in2out`:

 - If `in2out = TRUE`, which is the default and used in Example 1, element `x[[i]][[j]][[k]]` corresponds to element `x2[k, j, i]` (for all `i`, `j`, and `k`).  
 - If `in2out = FALSE`, element `x[[i]][[j]][[k]]` corresponds to element `x2[i, j, k]` (for all `i`, `j`, and `k`).  

The default of `in2out = TRUE` was chosen, because elements in subsequent rows are close to each other, while elements in subsequent layers (third dimension) are generally not close to each other, and the default of `in2out = TRUE` attempts to retain that behaviour.

For this example, the same list will be used as in Example 1:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
x <- list(
  group1 = list(
    class1 = list(
      height = rnorm(10, 170),
      weight = rnorm(10, 80),
      sex = sample(c("M", "F", NA), 10, TRUE)
    ),
    class2 = list(
      height = rnorm(10, 170),
      weight = rnorm(10, 80),
      sex = sample(c("M", "F", NA), 10, TRUE)
    )
  ),
  group2 = list(
    class1 = list(
      height = rnorm(10, 170),
      weight = rnorm(10, 80),
      sex = sample(c("M", "F", NA), 10, TRUE)
    ),
    class2 = list(
      height = rnorm(10, 170),
      weight = rnorm(10, 80),
      sex = sample(c("M", "F", NA), 10, TRUE)
    )
  )
)

```
:::



Let's once again cast this list to a dimensional list, but this time use `in2out = FALSE`:



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
hier2dim(x, in2out = FALSE) # check once again the dimensions
#> no padding no padding no padding 
#>          2          2          3
x2 <- cast_hier2dim(x, in2out = FALSE) # actually cast nested list into dimensional list
print(x2)
#> , , 1
#> 
#>      [,1]       [,2]      
#> [1,] numeric,10 numeric,10
#> [2,] numeric,10 numeric,10
#> 
#> , , 2
#> 
#>      [,1]       [,2]      
#> [1,] numeric,10 numeric,10
#> [2,] numeric,10 numeric,10
#> 
#> , , 3
#> 
#>      [,1]         [,2]        
#> [1,] character,10 character,10
#> [2,] character,10 character,10
```
:::


`x2` is the casted list.
Since `in2out = FALSE`, element `x[[i]][[j]][[k]]` corresponds to element `x2[i, j, k]` (for all `i`, `j`, and `k`).


Once again the `dimnames` need to be set manually:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# this time, in2out = FALSE
# so we go from the surface names to the deepest names
dimnames(x2) <- list(
  names(x),
  names(x[[1]]),
  names(x[[1]][[1]])
)
print(x2)
#> , , height
#> 
#>        class1     class2    
#> group1 numeric,10 numeric,10
#> group2 numeric,10 numeric,10
#> 
#> , , weight
#> 
#>        class1     class2    
#> group1 numeric,10 numeric,10
#> group2 numeric,10 numeric,10
#> 
#> , , sex
#> 
#>        class1       class2      
#> group1 character,10 character,10
#> group2 character,10 character,10
```
:::


There, the names are now correct.

One can print `x2` less compactly without much effort by flattening it, again using the [cast_dim2flat()](/man/cast_dim2flat.qmd) function.  
We only need to see a portion of the list in detail, so let's look at class1 from group 1 in the flattened form:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
cast_dim2flat(x2["group1", 1, , drop = FALSE])
#> $`['group1', 'class1', 'height']`
#>  [1] 168.7278 170.7973 171.2560 170.4654 171.0667 169.3453 170.4978 169.5738
#>  [9] 168.1899 171.2336
#> 
#> $`['group1', 'class1', 'weight']`
#>  [1] 81.20666 81.38403 78.92972 79.31318 80.33615 81.66615 80.71866 80.17757
#>  [9] 79.59866 78.95129
#> 
#> $`['group1', 'class1', 'sex']`
#>  [1] NA  NA  "F" "M" "M" "M" "M" "M" NA  NA
```
:::


 

## Example 3: Padding

For Example 3, we take the same list as before, but remove `x$group1$class2`:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
x <- list(
  group1 = list(
    class1 = list(
      height = rnorm(10, 170),
      weight = rnorm(10, 80),
      sex = sample(c("M", "F", NA), 10, TRUE)
    )
  ),
  group2 = list(
    class1 = list(
      height = rnorm(10, 170),
      weight = rnorm(10, 80),
      sex = sample(c("M", "F", NA), 10, TRUE)
    ),
    class2 = list(
      height = rnorm(10, 170),
      weight = rnorm(10, 80),
      sex = sample(c("M", "F", NA), 10, TRUE)
    )
  )
)

```
:::


Let's first check what dimensions it will get when casted using [hier2dim()](/man/cast_hier2dim.qmd):


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
hier2dim(x)
#> no padding    padding no padding 
#>          3          2          2
```
:::


The dimensions are the same as in Example 1: `c(3, 2, 2)`.  
But notice the **names** of the output are different: the second element has the name "padding", instead of "no padding".  
This indicates that some columns won't have enough elements to completely fill the column, and so additional elements will be added as padding.

So let's cast this list as dimensional:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
x2 <- cast_hier2dim(x)
print(x2)
#> , , 1
#> 
#>      [,1]         [,2]
#> [1,] numeric,10   NULL
#> [2,] numeric,10   NULL
#> [3,] character,10 NULL
#> 
#> , , 2
#> 
#>      [,1]         [,2]        
#> [1,] numeric,10   numeric,10  
#> [2,] numeric,10   numeric,10  
#> [3,] character,10 character,10
```
:::


Subset `x2[1, , 2]` is filled with `NULL`; this is the place where `x$group1$class2` was in Example 1, but since it's not there, we need to fill **something**.

To make it make obvious, let's give the array proper `dimnames`:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
dimnames(x2) <- list(
  c("height", "weight", "sex"),
  c("class1", "class2"),
  c("group1", "group2")
)
print(x2)
#> , , group1
#> 
#>        class1       class2
#> height numeric,10   NULL  
#> weight numeric,10   NULL  
#> sex    character,10 NULL  
#> 
#> , , group2
#> 
#>        class1       class2      
#> height numeric,10   numeric,10  
#> weight numeric,10   numeric,10  
#> sex    character,10 character,10
```
:::


Again, element "class2" is missing from element "group1", but not from "group2", and so padded with `NULL` when the list is casted as dimensional.

Sometimes, a different value than `NULL` is desired for padding.  
So let's change the padding with something REALLY obvious, using the `padding` argument:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
x2 <- cast_hier2dim(x, padding = list(~ "this is padding!"))
dimnames(x2) <- list(
  c("height", "weight", "sex"),
  c("class1", "class2"),
  c("group1", "group2")
)
print(x2)
#> , , group1
#> 
#>        class1       class2             
#> height numeric,10   ~"this is padding!"
#> weight numeric,10   ~"this is padding!"
#> sex    character,10 ~"this is padding!"
#> 
#> , , group2
#> 
#>        class1       class2      
#> height numeric,10   numeric,10  
#> weight numeric,10   numeric,10  
#> sex    character,10 character,10
```
:::


Once again, one can print or summarise `x2` less compactly by flattening it:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
cast_dim2flat(x2)
#> $`['height', 'class1', 'group1']`
#>  [1] 169.1494 169.0084 169.4902 170.5674 171.6746 168.5234 171.4246 168.2372
#>  [9] 171.0348 170.5815
#> 
#> $`['weight', 'class1', 'group1']`
#>  [1] 80.17487 78.78238 78.76462 81.75961 79.53171 78.91392 80.55407 78.64043
#>  [9] 79.08529 80.70651
#> 
#> $`['sex', 'class1', 'group1']`
#>  [1] "M" "M" "M" NA  NA  NA  "M" "M" "M" "F"
#> 
#> $`['height', 'class2', 'group1']`
#> ~"this is padding!"
#> 
#> $`['weight', 'class2', 'group1']`
#> ~"this is padding!"
#> 
#> $`['sex', 'class2', 'group1']`
#> ~"this is padding!"
#> 
#> $`['height', 'class1', 'group2']`
#>  [1] 170.6741 168.8564 168.5708 170.5317 169.6771 170.9603 169.2299 170.1458
#>  [9] 168.6807 170.6155
#> 
#> $`['weight', 'class1', 'group2']`
#>  [1] 78.61271 80.03006 79.88123 80.36043 79.98766 79.06312 81.02248 80.26045
#>  [9] 81.02684 81.85836
#> 
#> $`['sex', 'class1', 'group2']`
#>  [1] "M" "M" "M" NA  NA  "F" NA  "F" NA  "F"
#> 
#> $`['height', 'class2', 'group2']`
#>  [1] 170.1777 168.9846 170.3046 168.9651 170.4434 169.2505 168.7711 170.2313
#>  [9] 170.2084 170.2761
#> 
#> $`['weight', 'class2', 'group2']`
#>  [1] 81.56440 78.90411 78.95510 81.76903 81.56637 80.75503 79.87911 79.94208
#>  [9] 80.34554 79.85874
#> 
#> $`['sex', 'class2', 'group2']`
#>  [1] NA  "F" "F" "F" NA  NA  "M" "M" "M" "M"
```
:::



 

# Cast Dimensional List to Hierarchical list

'broadcast' provides the [cast_dim2hier()](/man/cast_dim2hier.qmd):  
[cast_dim2hier()](/man/cast_dim2hier.qmd) takes a dimensional list (i.e. an array of type `list`), and casts it to a nested list.

Consider the following recursive array as an example:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}

x <- array(c(as.list(1:11), ~hello, as.list(month.abb)), c(4:2))
dimnames(x) <- list(
  letters[1:4],
  LETTERS[1:3],
  c("group1", "group2")
)
print(x)
#> , , group1
#> 
#>   A B C     
#> a 1 5 9     
#> b 2 6 10    
#> c 3 7 11    
#> d 4 8 ~hello
#> 
#> , , group2
#> 
#>   A     B     C    
#> a "Jan" "May" "Sep"
#> b "Feb" "Jun" "Oct"
#> c "Mar" "Jul" "Nov"
#> d "Apr" "Aug" "Dec"
```
:::



Casting it to a nested list gives the following:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}

x2 <- cast_dim2hier(x, distr.names = TRUE)
print(x2)
#> $group1
#> $group1$A
#> $group1$A$a
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> $group1$A$b
#> [1] 2
#> 
#> $group1$A$c
#> [1] 3
#> 
#> $group1$A$d
#> [1] 4
#> 
#> 
#> $group1$B
#> $group1$B$a
#> [1] 5
#> 
#> $group1$B$b
#> [1] 6
#> 
#> $group1$B$c
#> [1] 7
#> 
#> $group1$B$d
#> [1] 8
#> 
#> 
#> $group1$C
#> $group1$C$a
#> [1] 9
#> 
#> $group1$C$b
#> [1] 10
#> 
#> $group1$C$c
#> [1] 11
#> 
#> $group1$C$d
#> ~hello
#> 
#> 
#> 
#> $group2
#> $group2$A
#> $group2$A$a
#> [1] "Jan"
#> 
#> $group2$A$b
#> [1] "Feb"
#> 
#> $group2$A$c
#> [1] "Mar"
#> 
#> $group2$A$d
#> [1] "Apr"
#> 
#> 
#> $group2$B
#> $group2$B$a
#> [1] "May"
#> 
#> $group2$B$b
#> [1] "Jun"
#> 
#> $group2$B$c
#> [1] "Jul"
#> 
#> $group2$B$d
#> [1] "Aug"
#> 
#> 
#> $group2$C
#> $group2$C$a
#> [1] "Sep"
#> 
#> $group2$C$b
#> [1] "Oct"
#> 
#> $group2$C$c
#> [1] "Nov"
#> 
#> $group2$C$d
#> [1] "Dec"
```
:::


The added `distr.names = TRUE` argument will distribute the `dimnames` in a logical way over the nested elements.

Like [cast_hier2dim()](/man/cast_hier2dim.qmd), `castdim2hier()` has the `in2out` argument, which (again) defaults to `TRUE`.  
As show above, the array `x`, with dimensions `c(4, 3, 2)`, became the nested list `x2`, where `length(x2)` is `2`, `length(x2[[i]])` is `3` for every `i`, and `length(x2[[i]][[j]])` is `4` for every `i` & `j`.  
Setting `in2out = FALSE` will cast in the opposite manner:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
x2 <- cast_dim2hier(x, in2out = FALSE, distr.names = TRUE)
print(x2)
#> $a
#> $a$A
#> $a$A$group1
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> $a$A$group2
#> [1] "Jan"
#> 
#> 
#> $a$B
#> $a$B$group1
#> [1] 5
#> 
#> $a$B$group2
#> [1] "May"
#> 
#> 
#> $a$C
#> $a$C$group1
#> [1] 9
#> 
#> $a$C$group2
#> [1] "Sep"
#> 
#> 
#> 
#> $b
#> $b$A
#> $b$A$group1
#> [1] 2
#> 
#> $b$A$group2
#> [1] "Feb"
#> 
#> 
#> $b$B
#> $b$B$group1
#> [1] 6
#> 
#> $b$B$group2
#> [1] "Jun"
#> 
#> 
#> $b$C
#> $b$C$group1
#> [1] 10
#> 
#> $b$C$group2
#> [1] "Oct"
#> 
#> 
#> 
#> $c
#> $c$A
#> $c$A$group1
#> [1] 3
#> 
#> $c$A$group2
#> [1] "Mar"
#> 
#> 
#> $c$B
#> $c$B$group1
#> [1] 7
```
